items.name: Halcyon-9
items.description: An aerosol sedative-agent seeded into indoor and outdoor air for four decades by the Clearline Initiative and its predecessor agencies. It blunts grief, pain, urgency and moral friction; people who lived under it call the state 'a comfortable distance.' It was never disclosed. Children exposed in the womb and in their first years develop dependence and 'latency syndrome' — endocrine and immune suppression the gas itself conceals.
invariants: Never publicly disclosed before distribution day.
Long exposure produces physical dependence that unmasking reveals as withdrawal.

items.name: Truebreath masks
items.description: Free, serialized respirators issued to every resident. After roughly six hours of continuous wear a mask bonds to the wearer's Haldane gland. Once bonded it filters Halcyon-9 completely; unmasked air then reads as physical assault — nausea, headache, panic. Adaptation takes one to three days and hurts. Masks are registered, replaceable, and rationed by household size.
invariants: The bond, once formed, does not reverse.
Replacement filters are manufactured from human donor tissue.

items.name: The donor program
items.description: Becoming a donor means surgical harvest of the adapted Haldane gland and surrounding filtrate tissue — the raw material for every truebreath filter and for the clean air sold to hospitals and institutions. Payment is one-time and scaled to assessed gland yield. The operation cannot be undone: the donor can never tolerate unmasked air again, must mask for life, and loses episodic memory of recent years with progressive flattening of emotional recall.
invariants: Consent is signed before the yield assessment, in writing, alone.

items.name: Priya Raghunathan
items.description: 38, night-shift pharmacy technician at Halvern General. Practical, tired, keeps lists. Under the gas she was steady and unremarkable and could not cry; masked, she learns she has been grieving her mother for eleven years and that her marriage was an anesthetic. She will trade herself for her son.
invariants: She keeps written lists and reads labels twice.
She never tells her husband about the intake number.

items.name: Theo Sandoval
items.description: 41, Clearline calibration technician, twelve years of service. Exact, quiet, loyal to procedure. Masked on the first day, he remembers a brother who drowned while he watched and felt nothing. Promoted into the donor wing because he does not flinch — until he does.
invariants: He never breaks protocol until he does it once.

items.name: Kavi Raghunathan
items.description: Six, born under Halcyon-9. Latency syndrome: immune and endocrine collapse unmasked by the gas's removal. Thin, bright, obsessed with the river barges and with counting. Survival depends on a replacement therapy only Clearline sells.
invariants: He counts objects and breaths when frightened.
He is the only person in the house who never knew the gas.

items.name: Dov Raghunathan
items.description: 41, warehouse loader, Priya's husband. Gentle and agreeable under the gas; masked, he finds a rage he cannot name and a fear of being seen clearly. Loves his son fiercely, cannot sit in a hospital chair.
invariants: He cannot stay in a room where someone is being told bad news.
He signs what is put in front of him without reading it to the end.

items.name: Sabine Okonkwo
items.description: Clearline's Halvern distribution director. Believes disclosure was overdue and the donor program is compassionate triage. Speaks in numbers, keeps a clean desk, has never worn a mask in public without checking the seal twice.

items.name: Halvern
items.description: A river city of four hundred thousand built around a shut barge works. Clearline Hall, a converted union hall on the north bank, distributes masks; the donor wing sits behind it in the old freight clinic. Wet air, iron bridges, cheap third-floor apartments that smell of the water.
invariants: Clearline Hall and the donor wing share a service corridor.
The river floods the low streets every spring.

items.name: Sell or watch him go
items.description: Priya and Dov must choose between irreversibly selling one of themselves and watching Kavi die at six, with the treatment priced at one gland apiece and a discount clause attached.

items.name: The man who files the forms
items.description: Theo must decide whether to keep processing donors at Clearline's wage, or to break the chain of consent in the only way his position allows.

items.name: Mother and son
items.description: Priya is Kavi's mother and measures every hour of her life against the sound of his breathing.

items.name: Technician and donor

args.viewpoint: Third person limited past tense, alternating chapters between Priya Raghunathan and Theo Sandoval
args.tone: Clear-eyed and close, tender in the household and clinical in the institution; sober, unsparing, quietly devastating.

chapters.title: First Breath
points: Theo works mask calibration at Clearline Hall on distribution day and watches the queue learn to breathe unfiltered air.
The first wave of sobriety arrives as smell, color and unmourned grief; a stranger weeps into a dead phone and a woman argues with a registrar about her son's mask size.
Theo masks at the end of his shift and remembers, for the first time in twelve years, watching his brother drown.
Closing tally: sixty-one thousand masks issued, four refusals, and a child carried out of the hall bleeding from the nose.

chapters.title: The Distance
points: Priya masks her family in their third-floor apartment and feels the anesthetic leave her marriage in a single hour.
Grief for her mother, eleven years unspent, arrives all at once; Dov cannot look at her and cannot say why.
Kavi's nosebleeds become something the night clinic cannot name, and Dr. Urdahl names it: latency syndrome.
The treatment exists and has a price; Priya reads the cost sheet and Dov says they cannot do it.

chapters.title: Withdrawal Weather
points: Theo documents the second week: withdrawal queues, unmasked holdouts in the low streets, fires on the south bank.
A leaked manifest shows replacement filters are made from human gland tissue, and Clearline stops calling it a rumour.
Theo is reassigned to the donor wing for his composure and walks the harvest suite in a paper gown.
He watches a donor wake and fail to name the woman holding her hand, and signs his reassignment anyway.

chapters.title: Arithmetic
points: Six weeks in, Priya counts what is left: a second mortgage, Dov's double shifts, Kavi's failing bloodwork.
The donor brochure arrives under the door; the argument that follows ends with Dov saying the true thing out loud.
Priya attends the donor seminar in the old freight clinic and sees what a donor looks like three months out.
She takes intake number 4471 and tells no one.

chapters.title: The Clear Room
points: Theo processes donors through consent, assessment and paperwork, and learns the comfort of other people's decisions.
Sabine Okonkwo defends the program with numbers; Theo asks what the numbers cost and gets a good answer.
He recognises Priya from the day-one queue and takes her file rather than handing it on.
Priya asks him what donors forget first, and Theo tells her the truth.

chapters.title: What We Agreed To
points: The night before surgery: Kavi's barges and questions, Dov's collapse in the kitchen, the two of them at the table at two in the morning.
The consent form contains a clause Priya must read twice — a discount in exchange for a registered future candidate.
Dov refuses to sign and Priya signs alone at four a.m.
She wakes Kavi before dawn and makes him say her name until she has it memorised.

chapters.title: Harvest
points: Theo runs the harvest suite on the morning he should have taken leave, and keeps his hands steady.
Dov arrives with the money from the truck, an hour too late and in the wrong currency.
Theo breaks protocol once, in the only way available: he records Priya's voice for her son.
The gland leaves in a cold case; Priya wakes and asks who the boy in the photograph is.

chapters.title: Clean Air
points: Kavi's treatment works; the flat fills with a stranger who keeps the lists and reads the labels twice.
Dov leaves in the spring flood, then returns for Kavi, and the house settles into a new and bearable wrongness.
The second letter from Clearline names Kavi as a pre-registered candidate under the discount clause.
Priya cannot feel the horror she knows is owed, so Kavi, seven, teaches her each morning to put on the mask and tells her who she is.
